roles.name: Internship
roles.summary: Learn fast, work safely in a real codebase, and ship small, tested changes.
roles.overview: An internship is where you prove that you can learn quickly and work safely inside a real codebase. Nobody expects you to design systems. Your team expects small, correct, tested changes, good questions, and clear explanations of what you did and why. Pick one main language and learn it properly; the concepts carry over to every language you learn later.
expect: Solve small, well-defined tasks in one language
Read existing code and follow data through functions and modules
Use Git, branches and pull requests confidently
Write basic automated tests and read error messages
Ask specific questions after trying things yourself first
tasks: Fix a small bug, starting from a reliable reproduction
Add a field or a validation rule to a form or an API
Write tests for a function that has none
Improve documentation or a developer script
Write a simple SQL query for a report

lessons.title: Programming fundamentals in one language
lessons.body: Values, variables, types, conditions, loops, functions and collections are the same ideas in every language; only the syntax changes. Learn them deeply in one language before adding a second. Practise by writing small programs from a blank file, not by copying tutorials: read input, transform it, print a result, and handle bad input.
langs: Dynamic typing and indentation as syntax. Lists, dicts and comprehensions cover most everyday work; start with the standard library.
Use let/const and === (never ==). Arrays and objects are everywhere; add TypeScript types early to catch mistakes before running.
Static types and classes from day one. The compiler rejects many mistakes before the program runs.
A deliberately small language: slices, maps, structs and explicit error values. Easy to read, fast to learn.

lessons.title: Reading errors and debugging
lessons.body: An error message is information, not a failure. Read the error type, the message, then the first stack frame that points to your own code. Reproduce the problem reliably before trying to fix it, then shrink it to a minimal reproducible example. Use a debugger with breakpoints to inspect values instead of guessing; print statements are fine for quick checks.
langs: Tracebacks list the most recent call last: read the bottom line first, then the frames above it.
Use browser DevTools or the Node inspector. Source maps map compiled JavaScript back to your TypeScript lines.
In exception stack traces, the "Caused by" section usually shows the root cause.
The Visual Studio and Rider debuggers break on exceptions; "Just My Code" hides framework frames.

lessons.title: Git and pull requests
lessons.body: Make one branch per change, keep commits small, and write messages that say what changed and why. Open a pull request with a short description and how you tested it. Treat review comments as teaching, answer each one, and push fixes. Never commit secrets such as passwords or API keys; if it happens, tell your team so the secret can be rotated.
langs: Ignore node_modules/ and build output such as dist/.

lessons.title: Your first automated tests
lessons.body: A test follows Arrange, Act, Assert: prepare data, call the code, check the result. Test the normal case, the boundaries and invalid input. Each test should have one clear reason to fail and run without depending on other tests. Tests that run automatically in CI protect you and your team from regressions.
langs: pytest: plain assert statements and parametrize for many cases.
Vitest or Jest: describe/it blocks with expect().
The built-in testing package; no framework needed.

lessons.title: HTTP, JSON and your first SQL
lessons.body: Most software talks over HTTP: a client sends a request, a server returns a status code and a body, usually JSON. 2xx means success, 4xx a client mistake, 5xx a server failure. Data usually lives in a relational database: learn SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, a simple JOIN, and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
langs: httpx or requests for HTTP; the json module or response.json() for data.
fetch() is built into browsers and Node; always check response.ok.
java.net.http.HttpClient and .NET HttpClient; map JSON to classes or records.
Practise on SQLite or PostgreSQL; the same basic queries work almost everywhere.

langContext: Python
The fastest start. Common in automation, data, QA and back-end internships.
TypeScript / JavaScript
The web: front end and Node.js. The largest number of job postings.
Java / C#
Frequent in enterprise internships. Static typing teaches structure early.
SQL
Needed in almost every role, because every application stores data.

quiz.q: Where should you start reading a Python traceback?
a: The last line: the exception type and message
quiz.e: Python prints the most recent call last, so the bottom line tells you what went wrong.

quiz.q: A field accepts 1–100. Which values test the boundaries?
quiz.e: Test just below, on, and just above each boundary.

quiz.q: You found a bug. What is the first step?
a: Ask someone else to fix it
quiz.e: Without a reproduction you cannot confirm that your fix works.
4xx codes are client errors; 404 means the requested resource does not exist.

quiz.q: Where do secrets such as API keys belong?
a: In environment variables or a secret manager
quiz.e: Secrets must never be committed; configuration comes from the environment or a secret store.

quiz.q: Which query returns customers from Poland sorted by name?
a: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY country
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'PL' ORDER BY name
SELECT name FROM customers GROUP BY name
quiz.e: WHERE filters the rows; ORDER BY sorts them.

exam.q: Which language is compiled to bytecode and run on a virtual machine?
exam.e: Java compiles to JVM bytecode, which the JVM executes.

exam.q: In JavaScript, 1 == "1" is true but 1 === "1" is false. Why?
exam.e: == converts types before comparing; === requires the same type.

exam.q: What belongs in .gitignore for a Node.js project?
exam.e: Dependencies are reinstalled from package.json and the lock file, so node_modules/ is never committed.

exam.q: Which is the best commit message?
a: Fix off-by-one error in page count
exam.e: A good message says what changed and why, in a few words.

exam.q: In Arrange-Act-Assert, what is the Act step?
exam.e: Arrange prepares, Act runs the code, Assert checks the outcome.

exam.q: What does HTTP status 500 indicate?
exam.e: 5xx codes mean the server failed while handling a valid request.

exam.q: What is JSON?
a: A text format for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null
exam.e: JSON is the most common data format for web APIs.

exam.q: What does an INNER JOIN return?
a: Only rows that match in both tables
Only rows from the left table
exam.e: INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on the join condition.

exam.q: What is a minimal reproducible example?
a: The smallest code that still shows the problem
A list of everything you tried
exam.e: Shrinking the problem often reveals the cause, and makes it easy for others to help.

exam.q: You have been stuck for 45 minutes. What should you do?
a: Write down what you tried and ask a specific question
Start a different task without telling anyone
Copy a random answer from the internet
exam.e: Teams value interns who try first, then ask precise questions.

exam.q: In Python, which structure is best for looking up values by key?
exam.e: A dict gives fast lookups by key; searching a list checks every item.

exam.q: Which file configures a Maven project in Java?
exam.e: Maven reads pom.xml; Gradle uses build.gradle(.kts).

roles.name: Junior
roles.summary: Own features end to end, write idiomatic code, and start reviewing others' work.
roles.overview: A junior developer delivers small-to-medium features with limited supervision. The step up from an internship is ownership: you take a ticket from an unclear requirement to merged, tested and deployed code, and you begin reviewing other people's work. You write code the way your language community writes it, and you understand the database, the CI pipeline and the most common security risks.
expect: Deliver features end to end with limited supervision
Write idiomatic code in the team's main language
Write integration tests and use mocks with judgement
Review pull requests and explain trade-offs
Work with databases: joins, transactions and migrations
Fix a broken CI build and recognise common security issues
tasks: Implement an API endpoint with validation, persistence and tests
Add a database migration and seed data
Find and fix a flaky test
Investigate a bug from logs and error reports

lessons.title: Idiomatic code
lessons.body: Idiomatic code looks the way experienced developers of that language expect, which makes it easier to read, review and maintain. Use the official formatter and linter, follow naming conventions, and reach for the standard library before adding dependencies. Translating another language line by line is the most common junior mistake.
langs: PEP 8, comprehensions, context managers (with), dataclasses and type hints; ruff for linting and formatting.
strict mode, union types, async/await and narrowing; ESLint and Prettier.
Records for data, streams where they are clearer than loops, Optional for return values that may be absent.
LINQ, async all the way down, nullable reference types and records.
gofmt, errors as values, small interfaces; accept interfaces, return structs.
clippy, Result with the ? operator, borrowing instead of cloning.

lessons.title: Modules, dependencies and configuration
lessons.body: A package manager installs dependencies; a lock file pins exact versions so every machine and CI run gets the same build. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) tells you whether an upgrade can break you. Keep configuration such as URLs and credentials out of code: read it from the environment so the same build runs in every environment.
langs: pyproject.toml with uv or pip; always work in a virtual environment.
NuGet packages declared in the .csproj file.

lessons.title: Testing beyond unit tests
lessons.body: The test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few end-to-end tests. Integration tests talk to real dependencies, such as a database in a container. Mock what you do not own (third-party APIs, email), but not your own database queries. Flaky tests usually come from timing, test order or shared state; fix them instead of re-running.
langs: pytest fixtures and Testcontainers for a real PostgreSQL.
Vitest with MSW to mock HTTP at the network level.
xUnit with Moq or NSubstitute; WebApplicationFactory for API tests.
Table-driven tests: one test, many cases in a slice.

lessons.title: Databases in application code
lessons.body: Junior work touches the database daily: multi-table joins, GROUP BY aggregation, transactions, constraints and indexes. Change schemas only through versioned migrations. ORMs save time but can hide an N+1 query problem: one query for a list plus one more per item. Always pass values as parameters, never by building SQL strings.
langs: SQLAlchemy for queries, Alembic for migrations.
Prisma or Drizzle, each with its own migrations.
Entity Framework Core and its migrations.
database/sql with sqlc, or pgx for PostgreSQL.

lessons.title: Async and concurrency basics
lessons.body: Separate I/O-bound work (waiting on network or disk) from CPU-bound work (calculating). Async code lets one thread wait on many I/O operations at once; threads or processes are needed for real parallel computation. Shared mutable state between concurrent tasks causes race conditions, and blocking an event loop stalls every request.
langs: asyncio for I/O. In standard builds the GIL limits CPU parallelism in threads, so use multiprocessing for CPU-heavy work.
A single-threaded event loop: await I/O, run independent calls with Promise.all, never block with long CPU loops.
Threads, ExecutorService and virtual threads (Java 21) for many concurrent I/O tasks.
Task and async/await; avoid .Result and .Wait(), which can deadlock.
Goroutines and channels; sync.WaitGroup to wait for a group of goroutines.

lessons.title: Code review, CI/CD and security basics
lessons.body: In review, check correctness first, then tests, then readability; keep your own pull requests small and focused. A CI pipeline runs lint, tests and build on every push, and a red build is fixed before anything else. Know the OWASP Top 10 basics: injection, broken access control, leaked secrets and vulnerable dependencies.
langs: npm audit; Dependabot or Renovate for updates.
OWASP Dependency-Check or the Gradle/Maven equivalents.

langContext: Python
Django or FastAPI, PostgreSQL and pytest: back-end, data and automation teams.
TypeScript
React or Next.js on the front end, Node.js or NestJS on the back end.
Java / Kotlin
Spring Boot, JPA and JUnit: large enterprise and banking systems.
C#
ASP.NET Core, Entity Framework Core and xUnit: enterprise, cloud and Azure.
Go
net/http or chi, sqlc and the testing package: cloud services and tooling.
SQL
Joins, aggregation, transactions and migrations become everyday work.

quiz.q: What is a lock file for?
a: Reproducible installs with exact dependency versions
quiz.e: The lock file pins every dependency version so all machines install the same thing.

quiz.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
a: One query for a list plus one extra query per item
quiz.e: Fix it with a JOIN or the ORM's eager loading.

quiz.q: A Node.js server runs a 5-second CPU loop inside a request handler. What happens?
a: All requests stall until the loop finishes
Node automatically moves it to another thread
quiz.e: The event loop is single-threaded; blocking it blocks everyone.

quiz.q: When is a mock the right choice?
a: For third-party services you do not control
quiz.e: Mock what you do not own; test your own database code against a real database.

quiz.q: An upgrade goes from 2.3.1 to 3.0.0. What does semantic versioning tell you?
quiz.e: A MAJOR version change signals incompatible API changes.

quiz.q: Why wrap two related UPDATE statements in a transaction?
a: So they apply together or not at all

exam.q: What is the idiomatic way in Python to make sure a file gets closed?
a: Let the garbage collector handle it
exam.e: A context manager closes the file even if an exception is raised.

exam.q: In C#, what is the risk of calling .Result on an unfinished Task?
a: It can block the thread and cause deadlocks
It turns the task into a thread
exam.e: Use async/await all the way instead of blocking.

exam.q: What is the Go convention for errors?
a: Return the error as the last value and check it
exam.e: if err != nil { ... } is idiomatic Go.

exam.q: What is Java's Optional intended for?
a: Return values that may be absent
exam.e: Optional signals "there may be no result"; it is not meant for fields or parameters.

exam.q: What is a common cause of flaky tests?
a: Timing, test order or shared state
exam.e: Make tests independent and deterministic.

exam.q: What makes a good pull request?
a: Small, focused on one purpose, with a clear description
exam.e: Small PRs get faster, better reviews.

exam.q: Where should a production database password live?
a: In an environment variable or secret manager
exam.e: Configuration comes from the environment; secrets never enter the repository.

exam.q: What is the trade-off of adding an index?
a: Faster reads, slower writes and more storage
exam.e: Index the columns you filter and join on, not everything.

exam.q: Which is an example of broken access control?
a: A user sees another user's order by changing the ID in the URL
exam.e: Every request must check that the user may access that specific resource.

exam.q: When should a CI pipeline fail?
a: When the build is too fast
exam.e: A failing gate stops broken code from being merged.

exam.q: What is a database migration?
a: Moving to a new database vendor
A versioned, reviewed schema change applied the same way in every environment
A manual SQL edit in production
exam.e: Migrations make schema changes repeatable and reviewable.

exam.q: What does the test pyramid recommend?
a: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests
exam.e: Fast, focused tests at the bottom; a few slow, broad tests at the top.

roles.name: Mid-level
roles.summary: Own components, make trade-offs explicit, run reliable systems, and grow others.
roles.overview: A mid-level developer owns components, not just tickets. You design interfaces and data models, make trade-offs explicit, keep systems observable and reliable in production, and raise the level of the people around you. You understand how your language's runtime behaves under load, and you can choose the right tool, or the right second language, for a problem.
expect: Design components with clear responsibilities and boundaries
Reason about performance, memory and concurrency
Lead the debugging of production incidents
Design test strategies, not only individual tests
Mentor juniors and evaluate tools, including AI assistants
tasks: Design a new module or service and record the decision in an ADR
Lead an incident investigation and a blameless postmortem
Reduce the p95 latency of a slow endpoint
Mentor a junior developer through a feature

lessons.title: Design and architecture
lessons.body: Good design keeps related code together (high cohesion) and dependencies few and pointing inward (low coupling). Put interfaces at boundaries such as storage, messaging and external APIs, so details can change without rewriting the core. Record significant decisions in Architecture Decision Records, prefer reversible choices, and start with a modular monolith before splitting into services.
langs: Explicit interfaces with dependency injection (Spring, ASP.NET Core DI).
Small interfaces defined by the consumer; implementations satisfy them implicitly.
Traits for behaviour; ownership forces a clear data flow through the design.
Structural types and clear module boundaries; avoid circular imports.
typing.Protocol describes duck-typed interfaces that type checkers verify.

lessons.title: Runtime behaviour and memory
lessons.body: At mid level you explain why a service slows down or runs out of memory. In garbage-collected languages, leaks are objects that are still referenced: unbounded caches, forgotten event listeners, static collections. High allocation rates cause GC pressure. JIT compilers need warm-up, so benchmark realistically. Use profilers and heap dumps instead of guessing.
langs: G1 is the default GC and ZGC targets low latency; heap dumps and JDK Flight Recorder.
A concurrent GC tuned with GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT; pprof for CPU and memory.
Reference counting plus a cycle collector; tracemalloc and py-spy.
V8 heap snapshots in DevTools; closures can keep large objects alive.
No GC; memory is freed by ownership. Watch for Rc reference cycles.

lessons.title: Concurrency and consistency
lessons.body: Distributed systems fail partially, so design for it: set timeouts on every call, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and make operations idempotent so a retry cannot charge a customer twice. Understand race conditions and deadlocks, database isolation levels, and optimistic versus pessimistic locking.
langs: java.util.concurrent and virtual threads; CompletableFuture for composition.
async with SemaphoreSlim and Channels; CancellationToken everywhere.
context for cancellation and deadlines; run tests with -race to detect data races.
The Send and Sync traits reject data races at compile time.
asyncio for I/O; multiprocessing or native extensions for CPU work.
Isolation levels, SELECT … FOR UPDATE, and version columns for optimistic locking.

lessons.title: Performance and observability
lessons.body: Measure before optimising. Track latency as percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages. Profile to find where time really goes, then fix the biggest cost, which is often a query or a network call rather than the code itself. Instrument services with logs, metrics and traces, ideally through OpenTelemetry, and define SLOs so you know when users are affected.
langs: pprof and the built-in execution tracer.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE to read real execution plans.

lessons.title: Test strategy and quality
lessons.body: A test strategy decides what to test, at which level, and how much, based on risk. Use contract tests between services so that one team cannot silently break another, property-based tests to explore many inputs automatically, and realistic, versioned test data. In production, feature flags and canary releases limit the damage of a bad change.

lessons.title: Leadership, mentoring and AI tooling
lessons.body: Mid-level engineers multiply the team. Review code in a way that teaches, write short design documents before large changes, estimate with ranges and state your assumptions, and run blameless postmortems that fix systems rather than blame people. Evaluate AI assistants critically: they speed up boilerplate and tests, but add review burden, and security and licensing decisions stay with you.
langs: A good second language for services, infrastructure and CLI tools.
For JVM services and Android, with full Java interoperability.
For full-stack product work with one language across client and server.

langContext: Java / Kotlin
Large, domain-heavy services; JVM tuning and concurrency at scale.
C#
Enterprise and cloud systems on .NET; high-performance APIs.
Go
Cloud infrastructure, network services and CLI tools.
Rust
Performance- and safety-critical components; systems programming.
Python
Data and ML platforms, automation and internal tooling.
TypeScript
Full-stack product development across web and server.
SQL
Data modelling, query optimisation and consistency in every stack.

quiz.q: What does p99 latency of 800 ms mean?
quiz.e: Percentiles show the tail that averages hide.

a: Repeating it has the same effect as doing it once

quiz.q: What is a typical memory leak in Java, C# or JavaScript?
a: Objects still referenced, for example an unbounded cache
quiz.e: The garbage collector cannot free objects that are still reachable.

quiz.q: How do you detect data races in Go?
quiz.e: The race detector instruments memory access at runtime.

a: A record of a decision, its context and its consequences
quiz.e: Architecture Decision Records explain why a system looks the way it does.

quiz.q: An endpoint is slow. What should you do first?
a: Measure and profile to find the real cost
quiz.e: Optimise what the data shows, not what you guess.

exam.q: What can happen when many clients retry immediately without backoff or jitter?
a: A retry storm that overloads the struggling service
exam.e: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out over time.

exam.q: How does optimistic locking work?
a: A version column; the update fails if the version changed
exam.e: Conflicts are detected at write time, which suits low-contention data.

exam.q: What does a contract test verify?
a: That a provider and a consumer agree on an API
exam.e: Contract tests catch breaking API changes before deployment.

exam.q: How does Rust prevent data races?
a: With the Send and Sync traits and the borrow checker at compile time
With runtime locks on every variable
exam.e: Unsafe sharing between threads does not compile.

exam.q: What does a blameless postmortem focus on?
exam.e: People act reasonably with the information they have; fix the system.

exam.q: What is property-based testing?
a: Generating many inputs to check invariants that must always hold
exam.e: The framework searches for inputs that break your stated property.

exam.q: Which JVM garbage collector is designed for very low pause times?
exam.e: ZGC targets pause times of around a millisecond, even on large heaps.

exam.q: What is a safe way to rename a column in a live system?
a: Rename it and deploy at once
Expand and contract: add the new column, write to both, migrate, then remove the old one
exam.e: Backward-compatible steps let old and new code run side by side.

exam.q: What is structured logging?
a: Logs as key-value or JSON fields that tools can search and filter
exam.e: Structured logs make it possible to query by user, request ID or latency.

exam.q: What does distributed tracing show?
a: The path and timing of one request across services
exam.e: Traces reveal which hop is slow or failing.

exam.q: Why does Go favour small interfaces defined by the consumer?
a: They decouple packages and make testing easier
It is required by the compiler
exam.e: The consumer asks only for the behaviour it needs.

exam.q: Which is a good mid-level use of an AI coding assistant?
a: Drafting tests and boilerplate, then reviewing them carefully
Letting it decide the security design
exam.e: Assistants speed up routine work; you keep ownership of correctness and security.
